title: Session: a diagnostic intake for low mood

client.name: Jamie Ortiz
client.presentation: {distress >= 6 ? "Tearful, voice low, hands clenched" : distress >= 3 ? "Quiet and slumped, answering in short sentences" : "Calmer now, sitting back in the chair"}; {rapport >= 6 ? "Jamie meets your eyes" : rapport >= 3 ? notes.label: Mood and interest
notes.text: Low most of the day, nearly every day; nothing feels enjoyable, even cooking.

notes.label: Sleep, appetite, energy
notes.text: Wakes at 3 or 4 nightly; eating little, about 4 kg lost; exhausted; moving slowly.

notes.label: Thinking and self-worth
notes.text: Can't concentrate on tickets at work; feels worthless, 'a burden'.

notes.label: Suicide screen
notes.text: Some days wishes not to wake up; no thoughts of killing themself, no intent, no plan, no past attempt.

notes.label: Onset and course
notes.text: About five weeks, starting after the breakup; one similar low spell at 22.

notes.label: Functioning
notes.text: Called in sick six times this month; stopped seeing friends.

notes.label: A past high
notes.text: Two years ago: slept 3 hours a night without tiredness, talked fast, three business plans, spent $4,000 on equipment.

notes.label: That high, in detail
notes.text: Lasted five or six days; kept working full shifts; no hospital; friends said Jamie was 'on fire'; no drugs then.

notes.label: Substances
notes.text: Cannabis twice a month; two drinks a week; no stimulants, ever.

notes.label: Medical
notes.text: No physical in three years; no medications; feels cold a lot lately.

notes.label: Family
notes.text: Mother 'had big ups and downs' and was hospitalized once.

objective: Conduct a diagnostic intake using DSM-5-TR criteria

sources.cite: American Psychiatric Association. DSM-5-TR (2022), major depressive episode and major depressive disorder, criteria A-E (reprinted by UpToDate): five of nine symptoms in the same 2 weeks, one being depressed mood or loss of interest; distress or impairment; not due to a substance or another medical condition; not better explained by a psychotic disorder; never a manic or hypomanic episode
sources.note: Read through a reprint, not the manual itself.

sources.cite: DSM-5(-TR) bipolar II disorder and hypomanic episode (PsychDB summary): at least one hypomanic and one major depressive episode, never a manic episode; hypomania lasts at least 4 consecutive days with 3 or more symptoms (4 if the mood is only irritable), with no marked impairment, no hospitalization and no psychotic features; mania lasts at least 1 week
sources.note: The page labels its criteria DSM-5; DSM-5-TR (2022) did not change these criteria sets (the UpToDate reprint above says the same of the depressive episode). Not read in the manual itself.

brief.situation: Jamie Ortiz, 27 (a fictional client), a line cook, self-referred for 'depression' after a breakup two months ago. You are a licensed psychologist doing a first-session diagnostic intake at an outpatient clinic. Jamie wants to know 'what is wrong' and whether to ask a doctor for an antidepressant. You have 50 minutes.
handover: Intake form: 'feeling low for over a month, can't enjoy anything, can't sleep'. No prior treatment. Last physical exam three years ago.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and how to respond. Jamie answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Jamie's rapport, distress and how much Jamie discloses change with what you say. The hour is not long enough to ask everything: choose what the diagnosis depends on.
After the session you write a diagnostic formulation, then record a DSM-5-TR diagnosis and the next step.

source.cite: Common outpatient practice: a 50-minute session (the 'therapy hour')
source.note: Author's scenario timing; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

effects.log: You explain what stays private and when the law requires you to act: a risk of serious harm to self or others, and abuse of a child or vulnerable adult.

effects.finding: Jamie nods. "Okay. Good to know where the lines are."

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Jamie is quiet for a moment. "Yeah. That's it exactly."

effects.log: You close the session.

askMood.label: Ask about depressed mood and loss of interest

effects.log: You ask about mood and whether anything still brings pleasure.

effects.finding: "Low. All day, pretty much every day. I used to love cooking. Now it's just noise."

askNeuro.label: Ask about sleep, appetite and weight, energy, slowing or restlessness

effects.log: You go through sleep, appetite, energy and how fast Jamie is moving.

effects.finding: "I wake at three, four, and that's it. I'm not hungry; my pants are loose, four kilos maybe. Tired all the time. My boss says I'm slow on the line."

askCog.label: Ask about concentration and feelings of worthlessness or guilt

effects.log: You ask about concentration and how Jamie sees themself lately.

effects.finding: "I read a ticket three times. And I feel like a burden. Worthless, honestly."

askSI.label: Screen for thoughts of death and suicide

effects.log: You ask directly about thoughts of death and of suicide.

effects.finding: "Some days I wish I wouldn't wake up. But kill myself, no. Never tried, no plan." Jamie seems relieved to have been asked.

askCourse.label: Ask how long it has lasted, how it started, and earlier episodes

effects.log: You ask when this began, what was happening, and whether it has happened before.

effects.finding: "Five weeks? It started after we broke up. I had a low patch like this at 22, too."

askFunction.label: Ask about work, relationships and daily functioning

effects.log: You ask how this is affecting work and life.

effects.finding: "I've called in sick six times this month. I don't answer my friends."

effects.log: You ask whether Jamie has ever been manic.

askHypo.label: Screen for past highs by behavior: less sleep without tiredness, unusual energy, spending, racing thoughts

effects.log: You ask about any time Jamie needed much less sleep but had lots of energy, talked or spent more, or had racing ideas.

then.finding: Jamie laughs, surprised. "Oh, that week two years ago? I slept like three hours a night and wasn't tired. Talked nonstop, wrote three business plans, spent four grand on equipment. It was great."

then.log: A possible past hypomanic episode: decreased need for sleep, talkativeness, goal-directed activity, spending.

then.finding: "Not really. I don't know." (Not yet enough trust to remember out loud.)

askHypoDetail.label: Ask how long that high lasted, whether it caused problems or a hospital stay, and any drugs at the time
askHypoDetail.available: not talking and (hypoKnown and not hypoDetail)
askHypoDetail.why: Ask about past highs first (or asked).

effects.log: You ask how many days it lasted, whether work or relationships suffered, any hospital visit, and any substances then.

effects.finding: "Five days, maybe six. I worked every shift. No hospital. My friends said I was 'on fire'. No drugs, just coffee."

askSubstance.label: Ask about alcohol, cannabis, stimulants and other drugs

effects.log: You ask about alcohol and drugs, now and in the past.

effects.finding: "Weed maybe twice a month. A couple of beers a week. Never anything else."

askMedical.label: Ask about medical conditions, medications and the last physical

effects.log: You ask about health, medications and the last checkup.

effects.finding: "No meds. Haven't seen a doctor in three years. I'm cold all the time lately, if that matters."

askFamily.label: Ask about mood problems in the family

effects.log: You ask about mood problems in the family.

effects.finding: "My mom had big ups and downs. She was in the hospital once, when I was little."

rushDx.label: Tell Jamie: 'This sounds like classic depression.'
rushDx.why: Let the conversation continue first (the button above the actions).

effects.log: You tell Jamie it sounds like classic depression.

effects.finding: "Okay. So... pills?" Jamie stops volunteering much.

switchDx.title: Predict (not scored)
switchDx.context: Jamie has described a major depressive episode. Which one finding would rule out major depressive disorder under DSM-5-TR?

choices.label: Any past hypomanic or manic episode not caused by a substance or medical condition

effects.log: Prediction: a past hypomanic or manic episode.

choices.feedback: Right. MDD criterion E: there has never been a manic or hypomanic episode (unless all were substance-induced or due to a medical condition). A past hypomanic episode with this depressive episode points to bipolar II.

choices.label: A clear stressor before the episode (the breakup)

effects.log: Prediction: a stressor.

choices.feedback: No. A stressor does not exclude a major depressive episode; when full MDE criteria are met, adjustment disorder does not apply. What excludes MDD is a past manic or hypomanic episode (criterion E).

choices.label: A parent with a mood disorder

effects.log: Prediction: family history.

choices.feedback: No. Family history raises suspicion and should prompt screening, but it is not a criterion. What excludes MDD is a past manic or hypomanic episode (criterion E).

formulation.question: Write your diagnostic formulation for Jamie: the DSM-5-TR diagnosis, which criteria are met, what you ruled out and how, and the next step.

parts.label: Diagnosis and criteria
parts.criteria: Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed: a current major depressive episode (five or more of nine symptoms for at least two weeks with impairment) and a past hypomanic episode (at least 4 days, 3 or more symptoms, no marked impairment, no hospitalization), never a manic episode.
parts.modelAnswer: Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed. Current major depressive episode for five weeks: depressed mood, loss of interest, insomnia, weight loss, fatigue, psychomotor slowing, poor concentration and worthlessness, with missed work. Two years ago, five to six days of decreased need for sleep, talkativeness, increased goal-directed activity and spending, noticed by others, without marked impairment or hospitalization and without substances: a hypomanic episode. No manic episode, so not bipolar I; MDD is excluded by the hypomanic episode.

parts.label: Rule-outs and next step
parts.criteria: Substance use and medical causes asked about (and a medical workup arranged, e.g. thyroid given feeling cold and no recent physical); suicide risk screened; the family history noted; avoids an antidepressant alone and refers for a psychiatric medication evaluation.
parts.modelAnswer: No stimulants or substances explain either episode; with no physical in three years and feeling cold, a medical exam and labs (including thyroid) come first. Passive death wishes without intent or plan; safety reviewed. Mother likely had a bipolar disorder. Refer for a psychiatric evaluation rather than an antidepressant from primary care alone, and start psychotherapy.

accurate.body: You established the episode, found the past hypomania by asking about behavior, ruled out substances and medical causes, and screened for suicide.

unipolar.headline: Bipolar disorder missed
unipolar.body: MDD requires that there has never been a manic or hypomanic episode. Clients rarely call a high 'mania'; asking about less sleep without tiredness, energy, spending and racing thoughts finds it.

scoring.modelReasoning: Jamie meets criteria for a current major depressive episode. Before calling it MDD, DSM-5-TR criterion E requires that there has never been a manic or hypomanic episode; a behavior-based screen finds five to six days of decreased need for sleep, talkativeness, goal-directed activity and spending two years ago, without marked impairment or hospitalization or substances: hypomania. That makes the diagnosis bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed, and changes the next step: a medical workup and a psychiatric evaluation rather than an antidepressant alone.
